passages.t: The anointed one: good news to the poor
passages.happening:
A voice speaks. ‘The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor’ (verse 1). ‘He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners’ (verse 1).

He is sent ‘to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn’ (verse 2), to console the mourners in Zion (verse 3). He will give them ‘a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair’ (verse 3).

‘So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This chapter stands at the center of the bright vision of chapters 60 to 62. Chapter 60 described Zion's glory. Chapter 61 introduces the one who brings it about, an anointed messenger. His words recall the Servant, on whom God put his Spirit (42:1), and the herald of good news (52:7).

Anointing with oil set people apart for a task: priests, kings, and sometimes prophets. Here the anointing is the Spirit himself. The Hebrew word for anointed, mashiach, became the title Messiah, and its Greek form gives the word Christ.

The word for liberty, deror, is the word of the jubilee law in Leviticus 25. Every fiftieth year debts were to be released, Israelite slaves set free, and family land given back. Whether the jubilee was ever fully kept is uncertain, but everyone knew the hope. This announcement is a jubilee.

Mourners put ashes on their heads. A festive headdress and anointing oil marked joy. In Hebrew, beauty, peer, and ashes, epher, sound alike, a play English cannot show.

Who is speaking has been debated: the prophet describing his own call, the Servant of the earlier songs, or a royal figure, since kings were anointed. These views can overlap. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a text called 11QMelchizedek joins Isaiah 61 with the jubilee law and looks for a heavenly deliverer who will proclaim liberty, so some Jews before Jesus already read the chapter of a future deliverer.
passages.later: At Nazareth Jesus read verses 1 and 2, stopped at ‘to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor’, rolled up the scroll and sat down (Luke 4:19-20). Then he said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).
passages.hard:
Why did Jesus stop reading in the middle of a sentence in Luke 4?

Verse 2 speaks of both the year of the LORD's favor and the day of God's vengeance, but in Luke 4:19 Jesus stops after the first. One common explanation is that he was marking his present ministry as a time of grace, with judgment kept for a later day, a pattern the New Testament follows in its teaching about his two comings. Others caution against building much on the stop, since synagogue readings could be short and Luke does not comment on it.

Either way, Luke does not deny judgment; later in his Gospel Jesus speaks of ‘the days of vengeance’ (Luke 21:22). But the weight of Jesus' arrival falls on favor and release.
passages.asks: The anointed one is sent to the poor, the brokenhearted, the captive and the mourning. Ask which of those describes you today. And ask what it would look like to receive a crown of beauty for your ashes, instead of hiding them.

passages.t: Ruins rebuilt, and priests of the LORD
passages.happening:
‘They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated’ (verse 4), the desolations of many generations.

Strangers will tend their flocks and foreigners work their fields and vineyards (verse 5). ‘But you will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God’ (verse 6). Instead of shame they will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will rejoice; everlasting joy will be theirs (verse 7).

God himself speaks. ‘For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity’ (verse 8). In his faithfulness he will repay them and make an everlasting covenant with them. Their descendants will be known among the nations, and all who see them will acknowledge them as the LORD's people (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The chapter speaks to a people of ruins, poverty and mourning. Most scholars place it among the community in Judah after the return; on the traditional view, Isaiah speaks ahead to them. Verse 4 speaks of desolations of many generations, ruins that had stood for longer than anyone could remember.

The double portion was the inheritance of the firstborn son. Shame is replaced not with a bare minimum but with a firstborn's share.

At Sinai God had called all Israel to be a kingdom of priests. Here that calling returns. The whole people serve as priests for the nations, and the nations care for their fields.

Verse 8 grounds the promise in God's own character. He loves justice and hates robbery. A people who had been robbed will be repaid.
passages.later: God had called Israel ‘a kingdom of priests and a holy nation’ (Exodus 19:6), and Peter gives the same names to the church: ‘a royal priesthood, a holy nation’ (1 Peter 2:9).
passages.asks: God promises a double portion instead of shame. Ask what shame you carry that God means to replace. And ask what ruin, in your family or your town, has stood for generations, and whether you believe it can be rebuilt.

passages.t: Clothed with salvation like a bridegroom and a bride
passages.happening:
A voice sings. ‘I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God; for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness’ (verse 10). It is like a bridegroom wearing a priestly headdress, ‘as a bride adorns herself with her jewels’ (verse 10).

‘For as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden enables seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a song of response. The voice may be Zion herself, or the prophet, or the anointed one. It rejoices because God has dressed it in salvation.

Wedding clothes were the finest anyone would wear. The bridegroom's headdress is described with a word used of priests, and a bride's jewels completed her wedding dress. Mourners who began the chapter in ashes end it dressed for a wedding.

The last picture is a garden. Seeds spring up, as the oaks of righteousness were planted in verse 3. The chapter moves from mourning to rejoicing, and from ruins to growth.
passages.later: A psalm sings the same change of clothes: ‘You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy’ (Psalm 30:11).
passages.asks: The singer rejoices because God has clothed them, not because they dressed themselves. Ask what it means for you to be clothed in salvation as a gift. And ask what God might be planting in you that has not yet come up.
